title: Like the vine
hookLine: a vine gives grapes and asks nothing more, so do good and move on (Meditations 5.6)
carry: giving grapes is what vines do

cards: You hold the door for someone and they don't say thanks. And there it is: a tiny flash of annoyance.
Or you help a friend move, carry the couch down three flights, and a month later you're still keeping score, just a little.
Plenty of people do good things and then hang around the good thing, waiting for it to be noticed. A new week starts today, called the shepherd, for a story coming in two days.
But first, Marcus has a picture for that little scorekeeper. It grows on a trellis.

teach.h: THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE WHO DO GOOD.
teach.b: In Book Five of the Meditations, Marcus sorts people who do good into three kinds. The first does you a favor and is ready to send the bill: you owe me.
The second asks for nothing out loud, but quietly thinks of you as in their debt, and knows exactly what they did. The third, Marcus says, in a way doesn't even know what he has done.

teach.h: A VINE THAT ASKS NOTHING MORE.
teach.b: He's like a vine that has produced grapes and asks for nothing more once it has borne its own fruit.

teach.h: THE HORSE, THE DOG, THE BEE.
teach.b: Then Marcus piles up more pictures: a horse that has run its race, a dog that has tracked the game, a bee that has made its honey. None of them calls everyone over to look.
They go on to the next thing, the way the vine, next season, simply makes grapes again. That's doing good as part of your nature, not a transaction.

Marcus imagines someone objecting: surely a decent person should notice what they've done? He grants the point, then warns that this is how you slide back into the first kind of person. The vine isn't being humble.
Being humble would still be about the vine. It's just being a vine. For Marcus, being helpful is what a human being is for, so helping isn't a favor you've done anyone.
It's you working properly, and the reward is already in it, the way the grapes are already the vine's whole point. Your line: giving grapes is what vines do.

how: Readers of Marcus often use this passage as a check on their own motives, and many traditions share a version of the idea that good done quietly, without keeping score, is good done well.

o: Marcus's picture of people tangled up in debts
Marcus's picture of a life that keeps on growing
Marcus's picture of doing good and asking nothing back

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: sends the bill: you owe me
silently counts you as a debtor
like a vine that asks nothing more

s: Marcus sorts people who do good into three kinds
the one who asks for payback, the one who keeps silent score, and the one like the vine.
the vine is Marcus's picture of humility
being humble would still be about the vine. it's just doing what vines do.
Marcus says the next season the vine makes grapes again
doing good isn't a one-time favor. it's what the vine is for.

games.q: you've done someone a real favor, and they haven't said a word about it. what does Marcus's vine do?
o: remind them, gently, what it did.
keep a quiet note of what they owe.
go on to the next season's grapes.
games.why: Marcus's vine gives its fruit and asks nothing more, then simply bears grapes again.

practice: Think of one small thing you could do for someone: refill something, fix something, send something, take a chore off someone's list. Picture yourself doing it, then walking away without saying a word.
Notice the part of you that wants credit, let it be there, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Vine, Marcus's picture of the best kind of good: it gives its grapes and asks for nothing more, then does it again next season. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, the language Marcus wrote in: the grapevine. Marcus's picture of doing good without keeping score.

carryVoice: Your line: giving grapes is what vines do. No bill, and no score kept. Until tomorrow.
